newsitem.title: USA: TWA debris said to point to mechanical malfunction.
newsitem.headline: TWA debris said to point to mechanical malfunction.

text.p: Officials investigating the crash of TWA Flight 800 said on Friday no evidence has been found indicating a bomb destroyed the jet but they have not concluded the crash was due to a mechanical malfunction.

The Washington Post reported that extensive metallurgical tests conducted on wreckage suggested that the Trans World Airlines Boeing Co. 747 crashed as a result of a malfunction and not because of an explosive device.

National Transportation Safety Board officials said metal recovered from the wreckage did not reveal that a bomb blew up the jet but they were not yet ready to make a determiantion of mechanical malfunction.
The Paris-bound jet exploded off Long Island, New York, on July 17, shortly after leaving John F. Kennedy International Airport. All 230 people aboard were killed.

Quoting senior safety and law enforcement investigators, the Post said detailed analyses of debris from the centre fuel tank showed damage patterns indicating a slower, less energetic explosion than that produced by a bomb or a missile.

They said the way in which much of the metal from the tank was bent, rather than shattered or pulverized, was consistent with a "low order" explosion or one that had less velocity and force than a bomb or missile detonation, the Post reported.
In addition, investigators said tests had shown that parts of the centre fuel tank were blown in an outward direction, indicating the blast occurred somewhere inside it, it said.

"From a scientific standpoint, the fingerprints that we have here are more consistent with a low order than a high order explosion," said one unidentified senior law enforcement official. "Clearly the burned and twisted metal is not indicative of C-4 (a type of plastic explosive) or other high explosives."
The officials said it was unlikely the board would make any determination of cause until all debris on the ocean floor was recovered. They sdaid about 90 percent of the plane ahd been recovered.
